article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Sativa-dominant hybrid
Genetics: The One × Sannie’s Jack
Breeder: Sannie’s Seeds
THC Content: 22%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Dark berry, grape, lemon, floral spice
Flowering Time (Indoor): 10–12 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: November
Indoor Yield: Up to 700 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Medium
Grow Difficulty: Intermediate

Killing Fields comes from a period of Dutch cannabis breeding when color, Haze-like potency, and unusual flavor could matter more than chasing the highest laboratory THC number. Sannie’s Seeds built the cultivar by placing The One—a private mother selected for berry, grape, blue-pink coloration, and deeper old-school funk—against Sannie’s Jack, a carefully worked Jack Herer line bred for vigor, heavy production, and an intensely cerebral high. The resulting marijuana became one of Sannie’s more recognizable creations, particularly because certain plants develop striking violet, magenta, blue, or pink hues beneath a dense layer of resin. Yet color was never the sole attraction. Breeder descriptions emphasized substantial yields, penetrating fruit-and-petrol aromas, and a powerful sativa-dominant experience capable of lasting far longer than its colorful flowers might initially suggest.

The strain also represents something increasingly uncommon in modern weed: a flavor profile that is sweet without tasting like candy. Dark fruit and grape emerge against lemon, floral spice, Haze, petrol, and occasional skunky or Afghan-like undertones. Long spear-shaped flowers and vigorous post-flip stretch reveal the Jack heritage, while The One contributes much of the darker fruit and pigmentation. Taken together, those characteristics make Killing Fields less of a novelty purple strain and more of an old-school breeder’s cultivar built around selection, aroma, resin, and a strong cerebral effect.
Genetics and Lineage

The direct pedigree is The One × Sannie’s Jack. Historical breeder material identifies The One as a particularly successful female selected from Blueberry Sativa × (Killa Queen × New York City Diesel ). Sannie chose the plant for its attractive architecture, distinctive blue-pink coloration, berry-and-grape fragrance, and a pungent undertone that became more noticeable when the dried flower was broken apart. That maternal line supplies much of the dark fruit, coloration, and unusual depth for which Killing Fields became known.

Sannie’s Jack provides the opposite half of the equation. Rather than using an unworked Jack Herer cross, Sannie spent multiple generations selecting his Jack line for a strong spicy-lemon Haze profile, large flowers, yield, potency, and a shorter flowering window than the longest-running Jack expressions. Historical breeder specifications for Sannie’s Jack list 10–13 weeks of flowering, yields as high as 750 g/m², and THC reaching approximately 22%. Plants continue stretching for several weeks after the light cycle changes, a characteristic that remains clearly visible in Killing Fields.

The first Killing Fields releases were subsequently worked into F2 and F3 generations rather than abandoned after a single cross. Sannie described later selections as an attempt to make desirable colored, flavorful phenotypes easier to find while retaining the heavy resin production and intense sativa-style high. This breeding history helps explain why growers have documented both green and deeply colored plants without treating either as inauthentic. Killing Fields is a population with phenotype variation, not a single clone frozen into one exact appearance.
Effects and Experience

The high is strongly cerebral and can be deceptive at first. Instead of producing immediate physical heaviness, the cultivar tends to build in the head, increasing sensory awareness, imagination, humor, and mental activity. Music can acquire additional detail, visual stimulation becomes more engaging, and ideas may arrive rapidly enough to make the experience feel almost Haze-like. Historical grow reports describe some phenotypes as overwhelmingly head-centered, which aligns closely with Sannie’s own characterization of the cross as delivering an intense sativa “up-high.”

That mental energy does not necessarily translate into conventional focus. In moderate quantities, experienced consumers may find the strain creative, conversational, and well suited to music, art, outdoor activity, or unstructured projects. Larger servings can make thought patterns increasingly nonlinear, with distractions becoming more interesting than whatever task was originally planned. Unlike heavily sedating indica marijuana, physical relaxation often remains secondary until later in the experience, although individual phenotypes and dose can change that balance.

Potency deserves respect even though the historical breeder ceiling of roughly 22% THC may look moderate beside current 30% dispensary flower. The psychoactive character is intense enough that excessive consumption can become uncomfortable for people prone to THC-related anxiety. Racing thoughts, short-term memory disruption, dizziness, dry mouth, and impaired coordination are possible. The long duration reported by growers also means impatient redosing can turn an initially manageable session into something much stronger than intended.
Medical Benefits

Killing Fields has never been evaluated in controlled clinical trials as a treatment for a specific disease, so medical claims attached to the cultivar should be treated as anecdotal rather than established fact. Its predominantly cerebral effects have historically attracted some medical marijuana consumers looking for a less physically immobilizing experience, while the later relaxing phase may be appealing to people seeking temporary relief from tension or discomfort.

Research involving cannabis more broadly provides some medical context without validating this individual strain. Cannabinoid products have shown modest benefit for certain forms of chronic pain, while research into sleep and other symptoms remains more variable. Those findings involve diverse cannabis products and standardized cannabinoid preparations, making it inappropriate to assume that Killing Fields will duplicate the effects observed in a clinical study simply because it contains THC.

A highly cerebral cultivar may also be a poor match for some patients. THC can worsen anxiety, impair concentration, alter judgment, and interact with certain medications. Anyone considering cannabis for persistent pain, sleep disturbance, mood symptoms, or another health concern should use actual product testing and appropriate medical guidance rather than relying on a historical strain reputation.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Dark fruit provides the aromatic foundation. The One was selected partly because of its berry-and-grape fragrance, and those qualities remain readily recognizable in Killing Fields. Breeder descriptions add a much sharper petrol note, producing an unusual contrast between ripe fruit and fuel rather than the sweet dessert flavor found in many newer hybrids. Crushing or grinding the flowers can release additional floral, herbal, and lightly skunky tones.

Sannie’s Jack contributes a second aromatic layer centered on lemon, Haze spice, and fresh herbal sharpness. Some green phenotypes have been described as especially lemony and floral, while colored expressions can lean darker toward berry, grape, spice, and fuel. This variation is one of the reasons older Killing Fields grow reports can sound as though they describe different marijuana strains : the underlying population contains enough genetic diversity for individual plants to emphasize different parts of the family tree.

No credible breeder-issued laboratory terpene panel survives for the original line, so it would be misleading to assign exact percentages to terpinolene, limonene, myrcene, or caryophyllene simply because those compounds could plausibly fit the aroma. The documented sensory profile is stronger evidence: fruit and grape from The One, spicy lemon-Haze qualities from Sannie’s Jack, and a pronounced petrol edge in the finished hybrid.
Growing Information

Killing Fields is a vigorous plant, and much of the cultivation challenge comes from managing that vigor rather than keeping the plant alive. Historical breeder instructions state that growth continues for roughly three to four weeks after switching to a 12/12 flowering cycle. Long vegetative periods are therefore unnecessary indoors and can create severe height problems. Sannie specifically noted that the cultivar responds well to topping and tying, making canopy training particularly useful where legal.

Flowering generally falls around 10–12 weeks. Older F2 breeder specifications list 11–12 weeks, while later F3 information places many plants closer to 10–11 weeks. That variation is best treated as a phenotype and generation difference rather than a contradiction. Indoor yield potential is substantial, with Sannie listing as much as 700 g/m² under optimal conditions. Flowers become large and dense despite the sativa-dominant structure, while resin can extend noticeably onto surrounding leaf tissue.

Color expression varies considerably. Many plants produce purple, violet, blue, pink, or magenta tissue, while others remain predominantly green. Genetics determine the underlying potential for pigmentation, though cooler late-flowering conditions can make anthocyanin expression more visible. Color alone should never determine harvest timing; trichome maturity, flower development, and overall plant condition are more reliable indicators.

Airflow becomes increasingly important as the long flowers gain weight. The plant may be relatively open during early growth, but large mature colas can create humid pockets if branches are crowded together. Supporting taller stems may also be worthwhile toward the end of bloom. After harvest, patient drying is essential because the bright fruit and lemon components can disappear quickly under excessive heat, leaving mainly petrol and earth behind.
FAQ
What strain is Killing Fields?

Killing Fields is a sativa-dominant hybrid bred by Sannie’s Seeds from The One × Sannie’s Jack. It became particularly recognized for colorful phenotypes, dark berry-and-grape flavor, petrol aromatics, substantial resin production, and a powerful cerebral high.
Who bred Killing Fields?

The cultivar was developed by Sannie’s Seeds, with historical breeder material crediting Sannie and Knutsel. The original cross combined two important selections from Sannie’s breeding program: The One and Sannie’s Jack.
What are the genetics of Killing Fields?
The direct parents are The One and Sannie’s Jack. The One traces to Blueberry Sativa × (Killa Queen × New York City Diesel), while Sannie’s Jack is Sannie’s selected and stabilized Jack Herer line.
What does Killing Fields taste like?

The central flavors are berry, grape, lemon, floral spice, and petrol. Different phenotypes can lean toward either dark berry-fuel or lighter lemon-floral Haze characteristics, while some display herbal or lightly skunky undertones.
How long does Killing Fields take to flower?

Most breeder information places flowering between approximately 10 and 12 weeks. The F2 was historically listed at 11–12 weeks, while later F3 material could finish around 10–11 weeks. Plants may continue stretching for three to four weeks after flowering begins.
Final Thoughts on Killing Fields

Killing Fields represents the kind of cannabis breeding that rewards patience. The cultivar does not finish in eight weeks, remain compact automatically, or produce a standardized clone-like population from every seed. Instead, Sannie and Knutsel combined The One with Sannie’s Jack and continued selecting through later generations to concentrate the qualities they valued: color, fruit, fuel, resin, high yield, and an unmistakably cerebral effect.

Its genetic foundation explains why the strain can be so visually and aromatically diverse. The One supplies berry, grape, blue-pink coloration, and deeper pungency through Blueberry Sativa, Killa Queen, and NYCD ancestry. Sannie’s Jack contributes vigorous growth, spicy lemon-Haze character, heavy flower production, and a soaring Jack Herer-style experience. The best phenotypes bring both halves together rather than merely resembling one parent.

For growers, the main requirements are room, training, and patience through the 10–12 week flowering cycle. For consumers, the reward is an older-school sativa-dominant weed profile that has largely disappeared from modern candy-heavy menus: dark fruit mixed with flowers, citrus, spice, and petrol, followed by a strong head-centered high that can remain active for hours. Killing Fields earned its reputation not simply because some plants turn spectacular shades of purple, but because the breeding behind those colors produced an unusually complete combination of potency, aroma, yield, and character.
